headline: AI coding speed study breaks: Developers refuse to work without AI tools
summary: A new study attempting to measure AI's impact on developer productivity failed to get clean data because many participants refused to work without AI. This highlights the deep integration of AI tools into modern coding workflows.
details: METR's initial 2025 study paid 16 experienced open-source developers $150/hour to work on 246 real issues. It found tasks took 19% longer with AI, despite developers believing AI sped them up by 20%.

A follow-up experiment, starting in August 2025 with 57 developers and over 800 tasks, could not get a clean answer. METR concluded its data gave an "unreliable signal of the current productivity effect of AI tools."

The main reason was recruitment: METR saw a sharp rise in developers refusing to participate if they had to work without AI. Additionally, 30% to 50% of participants chose not to submit tasks they didn't want to do without AI.

These selection effects likely led to an understatement of how much AI speeds developers up. Other issues included a reduced pay rate of $50/hour and unreliable time measurements for developers using multiple AI agents concurrently.

The 2026 data, despite its flaws, showed returning developers with an estimated -18% speedup (meaning faster) and new recruits with -4% speedup, reversing the 2025 finding. However, confidence intervals crossed zero, making the results inconclusive.

METR's own read is that developers are probably more sped up now than in early 2025, but this data offers very weak evidence. A randomized trial needs both sides, but fewer developers were willing to take the no-AI side.

A separate survey by METR (February-April 2026) found software engineers self-reported a median 3x speedup and would give up 29% of their salary to keep AI tools. However, METR cautioned that "survey results are not necessarily grounded in reality."

The 2025 trial showed people overestimated AI's effect on their time by 40 percentage points. The "stopwatch" (controlled experiment) is now hard to run because developers won't give up the tool, leaving only "feel," which has a known, large error bar.
caption:
Developers are so reliant on AI coding tools that a major study couldn't even run its control group. Many refused to work without AI, making it impossible to measure its true impact.

headline_marked: [[Cities move to regulate robotaxis]] as federal gridlock creates a patchwork of rules
headline: Cities move to regulate robotaxis as federal gridlock creates a patchwork of rules
summary: Frustrated by stalled federal legislation, cities and states are now creating their own rules for autonomous vehicles, leading to a complex and varied regulatory landscape for operators.
details: Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are now taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles. This shift comes after years of stalled legislation in Congress regarding self-driving car safety standards.

Initially, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars, eager to be seen as innovative. However, over a decade later, they are drafting new laws to manage the unintended consequences and ensure these vehicles follow basic road rules.

Washington's paralysis has resulted in local lawmakers creating their own playbooks, leading to a patchwork of rules and regulations. This outcome is precisely what many industry leaders had hoped to avoid, creating complexity for robotaxi operators.

While municipalities lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, they possess broad power over street operations. They are leveraging this authority to pass local laws governing robotaxi deployments and bring order to the chaos.

Examples include Minneapolis considering an ordinance requiring human monitors in AVs, effectively banning driverless operations. San Diego's City Council passed a resolution to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies control in emergencies.

Austin firefighters have also voiced concerns over the Tesla Cybercab's lack of steering wheel or pedals, advocating for dedicated rapid-response towing protocols. This pushback is blurring traditional political lines, with bipartisan support for stricter local control.
